name: 熊本ラーメン 肥後もっこす (Kumamoto Ramen Higo Mokkosu)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water; not gluten-free.
Paiku rice is pork simmered in a soy-based sauce, and tonkotsu tare typically uses wheat-containing soy sauce.
Broth is pork-bone based with pork and chicken items throughout the menu; no vegan-safe preparation.

name: くそオヤジ最後のひとふり 河原町三条店 (Kuso Oyaji Saigo no Hitofuri Kawaramachi San)

claims.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare — described as a blend of dark and light soy sauce over clam dashi — which typically contains wheat.
All ramen is shellfish-based (clam dashi with clam toppings); there is no vegan/vegetarian preparation, so cross-contact with shellfish is inherent to the menu.

name: 京つけめん つるかめ 六角 (Kyo Tsukemen Tsurukame Rokkaku)

claims.text: The dipping broth is a shoyu-based seafood/pork tare, which in a Japanese tsukemen shop is made with conventional wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.
Broths are fish (dried sardine/bonito) and pork/chicken based and chashu pork is a standard topping, so there is no separation from animal products for a plant-based diner.
Staff are noted for friendly, attentive menu explanations, so a diner with questions can ask about a dish before ordering.
Lunch ramen uses standard wheat noodles and shares a kitchen with motsunabe and fried sides, so wheat cross-contact is unavoidable; no gluten-free option is mentioned anywhere.
Broths and seasonings are soy- and miso-based (a soy-shoyu motsunabe option is offered), which in Japan normally means wheat-containing soy sauce.
Even the vegetable-forward cabbage 'hormone ramen' is built on beef offal and animal-based broth; all advertised bowls contain meat, clams, duck, or chicken stock.
Core dishes are wheat ramen noodles and a wheat-thickened curry roux sauce; gluten is unavoidable across the menu and no gluten-free handling is indicated.
Broth is chicken-bone based and the signature curry chuka is finished with braised wagyu beef; the kitchen is built around animal stocks and meat, with no plant-based option noted.

name: 京都中華 ハマムラ 府庁前店 (Kyoto Chuka Hamamura (Fuchomae))

claims.text: Wheat noodles, wheat-thickened ankake sauce, and soy/wheat seasonings are central to the menu; no gluten-free handling or dedicated equipment information was found.
Standard Chinese soy-sauce-based seasonings are used throughout; assume wheat-containing shoyu unless the shop confirms otherwise.
Broths and sauces are built on chicken-bone and kombu dashi with pork dishes prominent; shared woks and stocks make vegan separation unlikely.

name: 京都北山 元町ラーメン 四条烏丸本店 (Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen Shijo-Karasum)

claims.text: The bowl is built on a tamari/black soy sauce tare; tamari and standard soy sauce here are wheat-containing and central to the broth.
Broth and toppings are pork/beef based (beef tendon is a signature), so no item is free of animal products.

name: 京都らーめん おおの (Kyoto Ramen Ono)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles, gyoza, karaage, and fried rice are all cooked in a small shared kitchen, so wheat cross-contact is unavoidable.
The defining seasoning is a back-fat soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; Japanese soy sauce is virtually always brewed with wheat.
All bowls use a pork-bone broth with back fat and chashu; no plant-based option exists, so vegan diners cannot be safely accommodated.
